### 0002 — Essere fuori come un balcone

- **lit.** "to be out like a balcony"
- **meaning:** To be out of one's mind.
- **example:** Ma sei fuori come un balcone? Non puoi guidare così!
  — *Are you out of your mind? You can't drive like that!*
- **register:** slang · **exam:** avoid_in_exam · **regions:** it · **status:** approved

- **trap when producing Italian:** 'Essere come una capra' says something else in Italian — a capra is ignorant, hopeless at something, not crazy. Italian puts you outside instead: fuori come un balcone.
- **notes:** THE CAUTIONARY ENTRY. ### 0112 — Pagare di persona

- **lit.** "to pay in person"
- **meaning:** To take on yourself all the responsibility and consequences of what you have done.
- **example:** Il capitano ha sbagliato la strategia e ha pagato di persona, senza scaricare la colpa sulla squadra.
  — *The captain got the strategy wrong and took the consequences himself, without pinning the blame on the team.*
- **register:** standard · **exam:** ok_in_exam · **regions:** it · **status:** approved
- **source to verify:** Treccani → https://www.treccani.it/vocabolario/persona/ (headword: persona) ✓ verified
- **trap when producing Italian:** Two traps. First, 'dare la faccia' is not Italian — the face imagery does not survive the crossing at all, so the whole phrase has to be rebuilt. Second, and easier to get wrong: it is pagare DI persona. 'In persona' exists but means in the flesh, not substituted by anyone else — è intervenuto l'ambasciatore in persona. Swap the preposition and you have said the wrong thing.
- **notes:** Drafted by Claude 2026-07-25, replacing an earlier draft of this id that paired dar la cara with 'metterci la faccia' — rejected by Joe on naturalness. Italian side re-sourced from scratch. SOURCES NOT HUMAN-VERIFIED — read out of search results, so verifiedOn/verifiedBy stay null on both sides. Treccani glosses pagare di persona under the `persona` headword as assuming or undergoing all the responsibilities and consequences of one's own actions, with the examples 'siamo stati gli unici ad aver pagato di persona' and 'ha pagato di persona per la sua leggerezza' — the second is used here. ALTERNATIVES CONSIDERED AND SET ASIDE: 'uscire allo scoperto' (real and common, but its centre of gravity is revealing something concealed — going public, coming out — not answering for what you did); 'farsi avanti' (fixed but broader, closer to volunteering or coming forward as a witness); 'assumersi le proprie responsabilità' (accurate, no imagery, would be a collocation not an idiom). FOR THE ITALIAN REVIEWER: (1) Does pagare di persona read as dated or literary to you? It is the one thing I could not judge — Treccani's examples have a slightly formal ring. (2) Is the di/in preposition contrast a real learner error or one I have manufactured? The whole first interference note rests on it. FOR THE SPANISH REVIEWER: regions set pan-regional on RAE's authority — trim if it is not live in MX. ### 0241 — A nemico che fugge, ponti d'oro

- **lit.** "to an enemy who flees, bridges of gold"
- **meaning:** Ease the withdrawal of an adversary who is already leaving; a cornered opponent fights harder.
- **example:** Se vuole andarsene, lascialo andare: a nemico che fugge, ponti d'oro.
  — *If he wants out, let him go — build the retreating enemy a golden bridge.*
- **register:** standard · **exam:** ok_in_exam · **regions:** it · **status:** needs_review
- **source to verify:** Treccani → https://www.treccani.it/vocabolario/ponte/ (headword: ponte) — NOT YET OPENED BY A HUMAN
- **trap when producing Italian:** The metal changes at the border. Italian pays in gold and in the plural — ponti d'oro. 'Ponte d'argento' will be understood and quietly filed as foreign.
- **notes:** Drafted by Claude 2026-07-25. SOURCES NOT HUMAN-VERIFIED — both were read out of search results, not opened by a person, so verifiedOn/verifiedBy stay null on both sides. Treccani carries the Italian under the `ponte` headword and in its guerra-e-usi-militari proverb cluster; the Spanish has a full CVC Refranero ficha tracing it to Gonzalo Fernández de Córdoba with attestations back to Vallés 1549. ### 0314 — Il corteo dei Magi

- **lit.** "the procession of the Magi"
- **meaning:** A single historic Epiphany procession unique to Milan, not a nationwide custom: costumed figures walk from the Duomo to the Basilica di Sant'Eustorgio, pausing to reenact the Magi's encounter with Herod, and ending with gifts laid before a living nativity scene. Documented since 1336, tied to the belief that Sant'Eustorgio once held the Magi's actual relics — mostly carried off to Cologne in the 12th century, with a fragment returned to Milan only in 1903. Most of Italy has no equivalent civic parade for January 6th; the day's popular figure elsewhere is la Befana, not a procession of Kings.
- **example:** Il 6 gennaio, il corteo dei Magi attraversa il centro di Milano fino a Sant'Eustorgio.
  — *On January 6th, the procession of the Magi crosses central Milan on its way to Sant'Eustorgio.*
- **register:** standard · **exam:** ok_in_exam · **regions:** it · **status:** needs_review
- **source to verify:** Treccani → https://www.treccani.it/vocabolario/corteo/ (headword: corteo) — NOT YET OPENED BY A HUMAN
- ⚑ **REGION:** Specific to Milan. Most Italian cities have no equivalent Epiphany procession — unlike la cabalgata in Spain and Mexico, this is not a nationwide custom.
- **trap when producing Italian:** A Spanish speaker expecting every Italian city to have its own cabalgata-equivalent on January 6th will find nothing outside Milan — and even the Milanese corteo doesn't hand out gifts; it's a historical pageant, not the vehicle for presents.
- **notes:** Drafted by Claude 2026-08-15 at Joe's suggestion, as a companion to 0312 (Los Reyes Magos / La Befana) rather than a duplicate of it — 0312 covers who the day belongs to; this one covers the specific parade event, which is its own fixed collocation in Spanish ('vamos a ver la cabalgata') with no equivalent phrase on the Italian side. SOURCES NOT HUMAN-VERIFIED: RAE 'cabalgata' and Treccani 'corteo' are the general dictionary words, read via search, not opened by a person — note that RAE's own student dictionary entry for cabalgata names 'la víspera de Reyes Magos' directly in its definition, which is unusually on-the-nose confirmation for a general headword. THE HISTORICAL CLAIMS (Alcoy 1866/1885, Mexico 1975/Irapuato, Milan 1336, the Cologne relic theft and 1903 partial return) come from municipal, heritage-registry, and press sources, not from RAE or Treccani themselves — flagging clearly so no one mistakes secondary sourcing for dictionary sourcing. ES REVIEWER: confirm regions — cabalgatas are also established in Venezuela (1959) and elsewhere; I kept it to mx/es deliberately narrow rather than guess at the full list. IT REVIEWER: confirm the Milan-only claim holds — I looked for a comparable event elsewhere in Italy and found none, but this wants a native check, not just a search result. PLACEMENT: pinWindow 01-05..01-06 rather than a hard pin on either date, since the two halves of the pairing actually fall on different days (cabalgata = evening of the 5th, corteo = the 6th itself). Because 0312 already holds a hard pin on 01-06, expect the scheduler to resolve this one to the 5th in practice — deliberate, not a bug.

### 0316 — Un giorno sì e uno no

- **lit.** "one day yes and one no"
- **meaning:** On alternate days; every other day.
- **example:** Annaffia le piante un giorno sì e uno no, non tutti i giorni.
  — *Water the plants every other day, not daily.*
- **register:** standard · **exam:** ok_in_exam · **regions:** it · **status:** needs_review
- **source to verify:** Treccani → https://www.treccani.it/vocabolario/giorno/ (headword: giorno) — NOT YET OPENED BY A HUMAN
- **trap when producing Italian:** Almost nothing to correct: the Italian drops the second giorno, un giorno sì e UNO no, where Spanish repeats the noun as día then switches to otro. Both are fixed.
- **notes:** THE INCLUSIVE-COUNTING FINDING IS THE ENTRY AND IT NEEDS THE ES REVIEWER'S SIGNATURE. Mexican Spanish has 'cada tercer día' for what other varieties call 'cada dos días' — the Mexican form counts INCLUSIVELY (take it, skip a day, take it again = day 1, 2, 3) while the other counts the interval. Two WordReference threads document native speakers disagreeing about this at length, and a medical interpreter in one of them says they default to 'un día sí, un día no' precisely because the numbered forms get patients' dosing wrong. - **meaning:** Said sarcastically when one more unwanted thing arrives on top of everything else.

- **trap when producing Italian:** Italian wants the pronoun. 'Mancava solo questa' is grammatical and flat; the idiom is CI mancava solo questa, and the ci is what makes it sarcastic rather than descriptive. Note the tense too: Italian uses the imperfect, mancava, not the present.
- **notes:** THE ci/BARE CONTRAST IS THE ENTRY and it is my own reading — I claim Italian's ci makes the sarcasm and Spanish's bare form carries it without one. ### 0318 — Uffa!

- **lit.** "uffa"
- **meaning:** An exhaled sound of impatience, annoyance or boredom.

More importantly, Italian's version does not do relief: it is annoyance, impatience or boredom, and using it after a near miss will read as being irritated by the escape rather than glad of it.

- **example:** Ha pianto alla festa d'addio, ma erano lacrime di coccodrillo e lo sapevano tutti.
  — *He cried at the leaving party, but they were crocodile tears and everyone knew it.*
- **register:** standard · **exam:** ok_in_exam · **regions:** it · **status:** needs_review
- **source to verify:** Treccani → https://www.treccani.it/vocabolario/coccodrillo/ (headword: coccodrillo) — NOT YET OPENED BY A HUMAN
- **trap when producing Italian:** Double both: COCCODRILLO. Italian gemination is not decoration — it changes the length of the consonant when spoken, and a Spanish speaker who writes 'cocodrilo' has written a word Italian does not have. The same habit runs through the vocabulary: Spanish oficina against Italian ufficio, Spanish común against comune, Spanish atacar against attaccare.
- **notes:** Drafted by Claude 2026-08-01, batch 8 (CANDIDATES.md Freebies 18). CAME IN MARKED 'NO TRAP FOUND — shared classical ancestor, parallel structure'. The second pass found the gemination contrast, and this is the strongest of the six trap-free freebies: coccodrillo/cocodrilo is a real spelling error learners make, and it opens onto a systematic difference between the two languages rather than being a one-off. The cross-language examples in the es_to_it note (oficina/ufficio, común/comune, atacar/attaccare) are mine and unsourced — reviewers should confirm they are apt before they ship, since a wrong example in a note about spelling would be unfortunate. SOURCES NOT HUMAN-VERIFIED — headword URLs, not opened. NOTE FOR SCHEDULING: if the bank ever wants a themed run on orthography, this entry is the natural anchor for it.

### 0298 — Città natale

- **lit.** "natal city"
- **meaning:** The city where someone was born.
- **example:** È tornato nella sua città natale dopo vent'anni.
  — *He went back to the city where he was born after twenty years away.*
- **register:** standard · **exam:** ok_in_exam · **regions:** it · **status:** needs_review
- **source to verify:** Treccani → https://www.treccani.it/vocabolario/natale1/ (headword: natale) — NOT YET OPENED BY A HUMAN
- **trap when producing Italian:** Nothing goes wrong in production — città natale is exactly parallel to ciudad natal. The trap is in reading: an Italian text with lowercase natale is not talking about Christmas, and the capital is the only thing separating the two senses on the page. Note also the gender: Italian città is feminine and natale does not change form for it, since it is one of the adjectives ending in -e.
- **notes:** Drafted by Claude 2026-08-01. ORIGIN OF THE ENTRY: Joe's Italian teacher glossed 'città natale' as 'Christmas town'; Joe thought 'birth town' was more accurate and asked. He was right, and the research confirms it — Latin natalis is the older, broader adjective ('relating to birth', from natus/nasci), applied in Rome to birthdays AND to city foundations (Natalis Romae, 21 April). The Christmas sense is a fourth-century narrowing, so the teacher's gloss reads the youngest meaning back onto the oldest. THIS ALSO CAUGHT AN ERROR IN 0290, corrected the same day: that entry claimed Navidad and Natale come from the same Latin word, which is false — Navidad is from nativitatem, Natale from natalis. TYPE is collocation, not idiom: nothing here is figurative. If the bank does not want vocabulary pairs, this does not belong — same question raised on 0292 (Nochebuena) and the 'flor de Pascua' candidate row. THE ENTRY'S VALUE IS ETYMOLOGICAL RATHER THAN INTERFERENCE-BASED, and the es_to_it note is honest that nothing goes wrong in production; the risk is only in reading. Joe to decide whether that clears the bar. SOURCES NOT HUMAN-VERIFIED, and the Treccani URL is a guess at the disambiguated headword (natale1 vs natale2) — CHECK IT, since Treccani almost certainly splits the adjective from the noun and the entry should cite the adjective. The etymology in the bridge is corroborated across several independent Italian sources and Wikipedia, but no single dictionary citation is attached to it — if the bridge is going to assert Roman usage as fact, it should rest on better than that.

### 0313 — La novena di Natale

- **lit.** "the Christmas novena"
- **meaning:** Nine days of prayer and song leading up to Christmas (16–24 December) — the same nine days, marking the nine months Jesus spent in Mary's womb. In its most visible form, especially in the South (Naples, Sicily, Abruzzo), it is carried by travelling zampognari — bagpipers — who play from house to house or in front of nativity scenes; further north it survives mainly as sung prayer inside church. There is no door-to-door 'ask and be turned away' dialogue: the Italian novena is a devotion performed, not a story reenacted.
- **example:** Durante la novena di Natale, gli zampognari suonano davanti al presepe.
  — *During the Christmas novena, the bagpipers play in front of the nativity scene.*
- **register:** standard · **exam:** ok_in_exam · **regions:** it · **status:** needs_review
- **source to verify:** Treccani → https://www.treccani.it/vocabolario/novena/ (headword: novena) — NOT YET OPENED BY A HUMAN
- **trap when producing Italian:** A Spanish speaker looking for Italy's version of las posadas — a full street procession going house to house asking to be let in — won't find one under that description. The nine days survive in Italy as prayer and music, most visibly zampognari playing outside a presepe, not as reenacted door-knocking.
- **notes:** Drafted by Claude 2026-08-15 at Joe's suggestion (pair pedir posada with an appropriate Italian entry, if one exists). SOURCES NOT HUMAN-VERIFIED — RAE 'posada' and Treccani 'novena' read via search, not opened by a person. WHY THIS PAIRING AND NOT A LITERAL TRANSLATION: there is no Italian ritual matching the Mexican posada's door-to-door theater — I looked specifically for one (novena traditions, zampognari, presepe vivente) before settling on 'la novena di Natale' as the honest match: same nine days, same Mary's-nine-months symbolism per Treccani's own encyclopedia entry, same devotional root, but no reenacted dialogue on the Italian side. If Joe or a reviewer would rather NOT ship this pairing precisely because the traditions diverge this much, that's a legitimate call — flagging rather than deciding it myself. ES REVIEWER: confirm whether to widen regions beyond Mexico (Guatemala has posadas too, in smaller form) or keep the regionNote as the honest hedge. IT REVIEWER: confirm register — 'novena' may read slightly more formal/devotional than the colloquial energy of 'pedir posada,' and confirm whether zampognari is still the fairest example to lead with or whether it undersells how the tradition is actually experienced today, especially outside the South. PLACEMENT: pinWindow 12-16 to 12-24, same mechanism as 0077 (no year-boundary crossing, so the 0291 bug does not apply here). Because 0292 already holds a hard pin on 12-24 and 0290 on 12-25, the scheduler will place this somewhere in 12-16..12-23 in practice, not necessarily on the 24th — worth knowing, not a defect.

### 0329 — Le lenticchie di Capodanno

- **lit.** "New Year's lentils"
- **meaning:** Lentils eaten at the New Year's Eve dinner, usually with cotechino or zampone, because their coin-like shape is said to bring money in the year ahead.
- **example:** A mezzanotte non possono mancare le lenticchie con il cotechino.
  — *At midnight you can't skip lentils with cotechino.*
